messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Matthias Brandt is a 37-year-old German-American financial analyst who was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating occupational impairment and a recent separation from his therapist of two years, who had retired. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 59, consistent with severe posttraumatic stress. The precipitating trauma occurred approximately three years ago when Matthias was taken captive during a business trip abroad. He was held for eleven days in a series of confined spaces — a van, a basement room, and finally a concrete cell — by individuals whose demands were never made entirely clear to him. The conditions were degrading: he was kept in near-total silence for long stretches, occasionally broken by the distant sound of children crying somewhere in the structure above him. His captors handled him with an impersonal physical efficiency — moving him, restraining him, positioning him — that stripped him of any sense of being a person in their eyes. He was eventually released without explanation. No one was ever charged.

In the years since, Matthias has found that the world has become reorganised around a set of sensory thresholds he cannot control. The sound of children crying — something he now encounters regularly in the open-plan office building where he works, as a daycare operates on the floor below — pulls him immediately back into that basement. When the crying filters up through the ventilation system during the afternoon hours, his body floods with alertness, his attention fractures from his spreadsheets, and he finds himself scanning the room for exits. That same hypervigilance floods in when he encounters sudden, complete silence — the kind that falls when a conference call drops or when the office empties unexpectedly at the end of the day. Both sounds, and the absence of sound, function as direct activations of his threat system: within seconds of either, he is superalert, scanning, unable to locate safety even inside familiar spaces. He has difficulty falling asleep most nights not because he fears nightmares specifically, but because some part of him remains convinced that lowering his guard is dangerous — that the moment he stops listening, something will happen.

When threat is already elevated, his memories become harder to hold at a distance. Matthias describes his recollections of the captivity as possessing an almost hallucinatory quality — more vivid and present than anything from his ordinary life, as though the event is still happening in some layer of his nervous system. He can sometimes smell the damp concrete and the particular chemical odour of the restraints, and these sensory intrusions feel less like remembering than like being returned. The heightened state of arousal that accompanies his vigilance seems to lower the threshold for these intrusions, so that an afternoon of scanning and listening in the office can give way, by evening, to hours in which the memories press close and vivid against the present.

What the memories return him to, again and again, is not only the fear but the moral injury. Matthias has come to believe that he behaved in ways that contradict who he understood himself to be — complying, acquiescing, doing what was required of him to survive — and this belief sits in him like a verdict. He feels, at times, like something that was used rather than a person who endured something. The knowledge that the men responsible have faced no legal consequences compounds this: justice has not reorganised the world, and so the wrongness of what happened remains, in his view, unresolved and somehow still ongoing. These appraisals feed back into his sensitivity to the world in specific ways — physical affection, a colleague's hand on his shoulder, his daughter's hug during custody visits, reactivates the memory of being handled without consent, and the shame and dehumanisation surface immediately, making warmth feel like a threat.

Matthias sought help again after missing three consecutive custody visits — not because he did not want to see his daughter, but because the daycare adjacent to his ex-wife's apartment building meant that children's voices were unavoidable on arrival. He is most afraid, he says, that he will never be able to tolerate closeness again. What he is hoping for, more cautiously, is to stop feeling like the captivity is still in progress.
